title: Critics warned about Flock surveillance. Three Houston-area investigations are fueling those concerns.

reading.body:
This incident shows a failure of access control and oversight in the deployment of a license plate surveillance system. The system was built for law enforcement use, but an authorized user queried it for personal reasons over several years. The searches were not for official work, and the officer admitted the misuse.

The failure occurred at the point of use, where a human operator had broad access to surveillance data without a check that each query was job-related. Catching it would have required routine auditing of search logs against official purposes, or automated flagging of repeated queries on the same plates. The department's internal affairs investigation eventually found the violation, but only after the searches had continued for years.

What is not established is any criminal intent or illegal benefit. The lieutenant received an administrative suspension, not criminal charges, and the reporting does not show that the retrieved information was shared or used to harm anyone.

reports.title: Fort Bend County Sheriff's Office lieutenant admits to improper use of Flock cameras per docs
Critics warned about Flock surveillance. Three Houston-area investigations are fueling those concerns.

summary:
A Fort Bend County Sheriff's Office lieutenant improperly accessed Flock camera surveillance data between January 2022 and December 2025, according to internal affairs documents obtained by ABC13. The lieutenant searched one license plate 41 times and another plate 148 times, with searches unrelated to official law enforcement work. The officer admitted to the improper use but claimed the searches were motivated by concern that two drivers were lurking near their home and family. The lieutenant is not facing criminal charges and has not been named publicly.

An internal affairs investigation found the lieutenant violated the department's policies and received a two-day suspension. A University of Houston law professor explained that improper access to information constitutes an administrative violation, but escalating charges would require clear intent to harm or illegal benefit. The lieutenant claimed not to have shared the retrieved information with anyone. The incident comes amid growing controversy surrounding Flock cameras due to privacy concerns, with communities increasingly opposing their use and questioning their oversight.
